analysis.one_liner: Requires the Interior Department to sell oil and gas leases in a part of the eastern Gulf of Mexico currently withheld from drilling.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it died in a House subcommittee with zero cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill orders the Secretary of the Interior to hold a lease sale for oil and gas drilling on federal waters in the eastern Gulf of Mexico — tracts the government had deferred and not offered to drilling companies. Its sponsor framed it as expanding domestic energy production. It was introduced in July 2004, referred to committee, and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Oil and gas companies that would gain access to new federal drilling leases in the eastern Gulf of Mexico. The bill requires the sale without giving the Interior Department discretion to hold tracts back.

how_it_helps.text: It requires the Interior Department to conduct a lease sale covering all unleased tracts in the eastern Gulf of Mexico that had been listed as 'Leased or Deferred—Not Offered,' rather than leaving the decision to the agency.
Opening these areas to leasing would expand domestic oil and gas development in the Gulf, the primary stated aim of the sponsor's 'Energy Independence' title.

analysis.who_pays: The public, which owns these submerged lands, would bear the environmental risk of new offshore drilling near Gulf coast communities that depend on fishing and tourism. Because the bill mandates the sale, coastal residents would have no administrative avenue to block it.
analysis.who_pays_short: Gulf coast communities and the public

drawbacks.text: The bill hands drilling companies access to public waters that the government had deliberately deferred from sale, removing the option to keep those tracts unleased for environmental, fishing, tourism, or military reasons.
A mandated sale operates as a one-time directive; it does not address consumer energy prices in any direct way, so its 'energy independence' framing promises more than its mechanism delivers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefits flow mainly to drilling companies that would win leases; the costs — environmental risk to Gulf waters and the loss of the option to keep sensitive tracts closed — fall on the public that owns them. Even accepting expanded domestic production as a goal, mandating this specific sale with no environmental or military carve-outs is a poorly designed instrument for it.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Resources Committee and then to its energy subcommittee, where it sat out the rest of the Congress without a hearing or vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Christopher John of Louisiana introduced the bill on July 22, 2004.
The House referred it to the Committee on Resources, which referred it to the Subcommittee on Energy and Mineral Resources on July 29, 2004, and requested the Interior Department's views.
No further action was taken before the 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005, and the bill attracted zero cosponsors.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, the eastern Gulf tracts it targeted remained closed to new drilling, and the federal government kept the option to hold them back — a result coastal and environmental interests opposed to expanded Gulf drilling preferred. Offshore drilling companies, the bill's intended beneficiaries, gained nothing.

for.name: Rep. Christopher John
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill directing a mandatory lease sale in the eastern Gulf of Mexico.

against.name: House Committee on Resources
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its Energy and Mineral Resources Subcommittee and took no further action, so the bill never reached the House floor.

against.name: Subcommittee on Energy and Mineral Resources
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on July 29, 2004, and never held a hearing or acted on the bill.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and the bill had no cosponsors, so its support never took a partisan shape; the sponsor was a Democrat from a Gulf oil state.

industries.note: The bill would have granted drilling companies mandatory access to unleased eastern Gulf tracts the government had withheld. Its failure means the industry gained nothing, while the public kept the tracts closed — one of the rare cases where the outcome favored ordinary people over a concentrated interest.

industries.industry: Gulf coast tourism and commercial fishing
industries.note: New drilling near the eastern Gulf would have put spill risk alongside communities dependent on beaches and fisheries. The bill's death preserved the status quo for them.
